# SafeBAE 360º Schools

#### Tools, Training, and Youth Leadership to Build Safer School Communities — Together

SafeBAE 360° is a comprehensive, survivor-centered prevention model that reimagines how schools address sexual and dating violence. Created by and for young people, the program builds lasting infrastructure for prevention — spanning education, leadership, policy, reporting, and accountability — so that every student has access to support, and every school has the tools to respond.

Rather than treating students as passive recipients of adult-designed interventions, SafeBAE 360° equips young people to lead. Each implementation is adapted to the school’s specific context — prioritizing cultural relevance, sustainability, and alignment with the needs of those most impacted.

Whether implemented in full or through individual components, SafeBAE 360° is rooted in the belief that real prevention requires collective and sustained change.

#### Flexible Prevention Programming for Schools

We’d love to connect! Whether you’re ready to explore full implementation or just looking for a starting point, we offer flexible options to meet your school’s needs.

Some partners begin with a single assembly or awareness event, while others dive into a deeper collaboration right away. Wherever you begin, we can help you take actionable steps toward building safer, more supportive school environments.

**Let’s Start the Conversation.**

[Request a Program](https://www.safebae.org/request-a-program/ "Request a Program")

[Explore Our Resources](https://www.safebae.org/resources/ "Resources")

[Shop Educational Products](https://safebae.podia.com/ "Shop Educational Products")

### SafeBAE 360° includes six core components that work together to create lasting, schoolwide culture change — where prevention, support, and accountability are embedded in everyday life. Each component can also be implemented on its own, depending on a school’s needs.

* [**Peer Educator Training & Youth Leadership**](https://www.safebae.org/resources/peer-educator-training/)  
  Students complete a self-paced, online certification to become Peer Educators, equipping them with the knowledge, skills, and support to lead prevention efforts in their schools. Youth leaders help shape implementation, lead presentations, co-facilitate curriculum sessions, organize campaigns through SafeBAE Clubs, and receive ongoing mentorship from our team.
* [**Healthy Relationship & Consent Curriculum**](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/consent-curriculum/)  
  A 16-module, trauma-informed curriculum aligned with the National Health Education Standards. Lessons cover consent, boundaries, communication, digital safety, healing, and accountability. Schools receive a complete curriculum package — including lesson plans, slides, activities, and printable resources — delivered by teachers and peer educators with support from our team.
* [**Faculty and Staff Training**](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/professional-development/)  
  Professional development for teachers, staff, and administrators focuses on trauma-informed response, supporting marginalized students, and building a school culture of consent and accountability. Trainings are flexible and tailored to school contexts.
* [**School Policy Support**](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/school-policy-reform-guide/)  
  Hands-on consultation helps schools audit and revise sexual misconduct and Title IX policies. Support includes annotated audits, student-centered model language, communication templates, and rollout strategies to ensure policies are accessible, compliant, trusted, and trauma-informed.
* [**Anonymous Reporting Tool (SafeBAE x REES)**](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/professional-development/)  
  A secure, private space where students can document incidents of harm or violence at their own pace. Students have the option to report anonymously or by name directly to their school, and are connected with school-specific resources and support. Schools can partner with SafeBAE and REES to implement this tool — creating a trusted, customized reporting system that works for their community.
* [**Educational Resources to Reduce Recidivism**](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/accountability-training/)  
  A suite of tools designed for students who have caused harm, supporting education, accountability, and behavior change. This component includes our structured Accountability Training as well as [Vibe Check](http://checkyourvibe.org), a self-assessment tool that helps students recognize unhealthy relationship behaviors and warning signs in themselves. Rooted in principles of prevention, healing, and restorative justice — not punishment — these resources offer schools a trauma-informed, developmentally appropriate alternative to traditional disciplinary responses.

## Making an Immediate Impact

*“I wanted to give you some uplifting news, I was talking with my intern from the school you visited and she informed me that the presentation that you did really affected the youth at the school. In fact, she has friends that are a couple, and they were in an unhealthy relationship and your presentation changed the way they now treat one another. She also said that she was able to look at herself and how she treated her partner and make changes as well. I wanted you to know that you really make a difference and thank you, once more for touching the lives of our youth.”*

– Dawn M. Keys, Newport Prevention Coalition Coordinator

### Data Driven Programs

We believe that prevention should always be youth-led and evidence-driven. That’s why we collect data — to understand our impact and ensure we’re truly reaching students, shifting school culture, and building the skills and confidence young people need to create safer communities. Our findings come from ongoing evaluations, youth-designed surveys, internal assessments, and published research.

# Accountability Training for Schools

Historically, schools, universities, and courts across the country have had virtually no resources to address students accused of or found responsible for sexual assault. In most Title IX cases, the primary resolution has been suspension or expulsion.

But in our work with survivors, we often hear how traumatizing and difficult investigations can be — and how many survivors want alternatives. Some would like resolution options that focus on accountability and healing rather than only punishment. The operative word is **choice**: survivors must be free to decide what path feels safest and most meaningful for them. Not all will choose these alternatives, but again and again we hear two consistent requests: ***“I want them to apologize, and I want them to not do this to anyone else.”***

In our ongoing mission to provide resources for both prevention and response, we developed this training specifically for students who have harmed another student. It is designed to help them reflect on intention versus outcome, identify harmful behaviors, and reduce the likelihood of reoffending.

## What the Training Covers

Through a comprehensive multi-lesson virtual program, participants are guided through core topics, including:

* + How to Respond If You’ve Been Accused
  + The Origins of Rape Culture
  + Sexual Assault, Harassment, and Rape – Defined
  + Consent
  + Healthy Relationships
  + Male Youth & Sexual Violence
  + Myths, Facts & Statistics
  + Sexual Violence & Relationships in Media
  + Online Safety & Sending Nudes
  + Healing After Sexual Violence
  + Dating Someone Who Has Experienced Sexual Violence
  + Bystander Intervention

Each lesson is followed by a knowledge check to ensure understanding.

[Learn More](https://safebae.podia.com/7db95b2a-0fc8-47a7-b4f2-69c2a01232a9)

## Additional Information

* **Languages**: Currently available in English and Spanish.
* **Development**: Created by experts in partnership with young survivors, ensuring authenticity, effectiveness, and relevance. As with all of our programs, we welcome feedback to continuously improve and expand inclusivity.
* **Access**: Available for purchase through either an annual unlimited-use license or a single-use license.

# Healthy Relationship & Consent Curriculum

Our flexible, trauma-informed curriculum includes 15 interactive modules aligned with the National Health Education Standards (NHES). Lessons explore consent, communication, boundaries, digital safety, survivor support, healing, and more.

Developed with youth and expert collaborators, the curriculum also includes modules on sexting and tech-facilitated abuse, dating after sexual assault, and accountability for those who’ve caused harm. Content is available in English and Spanish and can be facilitated by teachers, co-taught with peer educators, or delivered directly by our team.

Schools receive a complete curriculum package that includes:

* Full lesson plans and facilitation guides
* Slide decks and multimedia materials
* Posters and printable resources
* Assessments and interactive activities

This comprehensive package ensures schools can deliver engaging, developmentally appropriate prevention education with clarity, consistency, and care.

[Consent Curriculum | Podia](https://safebae.podia.com/ "Consent Curriculum | Podia")

### Curriculum Facilitator's Guide Preview

SafeBAE’s curriculum is engaging, interactive, and most importantly youth-centered. SafeBAE worked with student leaders to develop each lesson which includes visual slides with content and videos for student engagement as well as a facilitators guide.

Each lesson can run between 45 – 60 mins, with learning objectives and knowledge checks included for students. Facilitators of the curriculum are encouraged to bring their voice and teaching style to each lesson but may find the slide by slide facilitator guide helpful in leading the conversation. SafeBAE encourages curiosity and questions as the curriculum focusses on important and sensitive topics. We’re happy to help field any training and technical assistance requests via email at [info@www.safebae.org](mailto:info@www.safebae.org).

## Curriculum Structure & Contents

The curriculum is designed to address core concepts related to healthy relationship education and sexual violence prevention. Each lesson includes visual slides, interactive video content, and other talking points to engage students in learning. The curriculum is divided into 15 modules or lessons.

**Core Concepts: Lessons One-Six**

Basic concepts to address with students related to dating violence, sexual violence, and healthy relationships.

* 1: Healthy Relationships
* 2: Consent
* 3: Online Safety & Sending Nudes
* 4: Bystander Intervention
* 5. Male Youth & Sexual Violence
* 6. If You’ve Been Accused of Sexual Assault

**Foundational Knowledge: Lessons Seven-Ten**

Foundations of understanding sexual violence, expanding on definitions of crimes, and the influence of media, pop culture, and myths.

* 7. Rape Culture
* 8. Sexual Harassment, Assault, Rape – Defined
* 9. Violence in the Media
* 10. Myths, Facts & Stats

**Healing Resources: Lessons Eleven-Thirteen**

Focus on victim support and healing after incidents of violence, including how peers can support survivors and how individuals can take steps towards healing and moving forward in new relationships.

* 11. Healing After Sexual Violence
* 12. Support a Survivor
* 13. Dating After Violence

**Justice Options: Lessons Fourteen-Fifteen**

Review of options for justice after experiencing violence with a focus on victim autonomy, review of Title IX policies and procedures, as well as other methods for reporting crimes.

* 14. Title IX
* 15. Options for Reporting

# School Sexual Misconduct Policy Reform Guide

## Help Reform Your School's Sexual Misconduct Policy

Strong, trauma-informed policies are the foundation of a safe school community. Yet since 2020, shifting federal Title IX regulations have left schools caught in the middle of inconsistent rules, legal challenges, and unclear enforcement. The 2020 rule narrowed protections for survivors and restricted schools’ ability to respond effectively. While 2024 guidelines attempted to restore protections, they were quickly tied up in court — forcing most schools back under the restrictive 2020 rule.

This federal uncertainty leaves both students and school districts vulnerable: survivors face heightened risk of further harm, and administrators face potential legal exposure without clear, stable standards to follow.

That’s why SafeBAE developed the **School Policy Reform Guide** — a step-by-step resource to help administrators, faculty, and district leaders strengthen their policies beyond the bare federal minimum. Grounded in trauma-informed practice and survivor-centered values, this guide walks you through building policies that promote transparency, accountability, and safety for every student.

By proactively strengthening your school’s policies, you not only protect students — you also safeguard your institution and demonstrate leadership in creating safer, healthier learning environments.

# About SafeBAE

### **Our Mission: Survivor-Founded, Youth-Led**

SafeBAE is the only survivor-founded, youth-led organization working to end sexual violence among middle and high school students nationwide. We equip young people with the tools to prevent harm, support their peers, and drive generational culture change — strengthening mental health, uplifting youth leadership, and creating safer school communities.

[Support Our Work](https://www.safebae.org/donate/ "Donate")

[Explore Our Resources](https://www.safebae.org/resources/ "Resources")

## Our Story

At SafeBAE, we believe rape culture and sexual assault are among the most dangerous and life-altering issues facing young people today, compounded by a growing and interconnected youth mental health crisis. Despite alarming rates of sexual violence among youth — higher than any other age group — our schools continue to offer little in the way of education or tools to prevent it.

We founded SafeBAE in 2015 because we knew that had to change. Daisy, Ella, and Jada — teen survivors of sexual assault — came together with Daisy’s brother, Charlie, and our Executive Director, Shael, to build something we never had: a way to stop what happened to us from happening to anyone else. The “BAE” in SafeBAE stands for Before Anyone Else — because we know prevention has to start early.

The idea for SafeBAE began during the filming of the Peabody Award-winning Netflix documentary [*Audrie & Daisy*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audrie_%26_Daisy). As we shared our stories, one devastating truth became clear: none of us had ever received meaningful education about consent, Title IX, or how to recognize and prevent sexual violence. That knowledge gap was the common thread in our experiences, and it’s exactly what we set out to change.

We knew the work couldn’t wait until college. It had to begin earlier, in middle and high school, when beliefs about intimacy, boundaries, and safety are just beginning to form. SafeBAE exists to fill that gap: to empower young people before harm happens, and when it does, to ensure they have access to survivor-centered care, community, and lasting support.

# Our Impact: Data, Findings, & Learning

At SafeBAE, we believe that sexual violence prevention should always be youth-led and evidence-driven. That’s why we collect data — to understand our impact and ensure we’re truly reaching students, shifting school culture, and building the skills and confidence young people need to create safer communities. Our findings come from ongoing evaluations, youth-designed surveys, internal assessments, and published research.

We’re committed to transparency, ongoing learning, and accountability to the youth and communities we serve. Want to explore who we collaborate with? Visit our [Partners & Press](https://www.safebae.org/partners-press/) page.

### SafeBAE's Research Published

Most school-based sexual violence prevention programs are not evidence-based — and even fewer are designed with or by young people. At SafeBAE, we’re building something different: prevention rooted in youth leadership, survivor-centered programming, and real-world data. Our evaluation efforts ensure our model is effective, equitable, and responsive to the communities we serve.

This commitment to rigor led to our research being published in the *Journal of Child Sexual Abuse*. Co-authored by our Executive Director, Shael Norris, with Dr. Lindsay Orchowski and Dr. Prachi Bhuptani of Brown University, Rhode Island Hospital, and Lifespan Hospital, the study shows that SafeBAE’s approach to preventing sexual violence isn’t just effective — it’s transformative.

## 2023 Program Efficacy Data

Since our founding in 2015, SafeBAE has been committed to collecting and analyzing data across all programs and projects. With the guidance of our research partners, we have published dedicated evaluations and shared qualitative insights in our annual reports. We are especially proud to share the findings from our most recent evaluation of the Certified Peer Educator Training, which demonstrate the program’s unprecedented impact on both the knowledge and actions of participating students.

### Climate Survey

Since 2015, our work with thousands of students has confirmed what the data now makes undeniable: sexual violence is at crisis levels for teens across the country. While the [CDC’s Youth Risk Behavior Survey](https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/results/2023-yrbs-results.html) underscores the severity of this issue, SafeBAE has sought deeper insights into how it plays out in schools every day.

Through the **SafeBAE National School Sexual Violence Climate Survey (2020–23)**, we partnered with students and schools to capture the lived realities of school culture — focusing on safety, support systems, and institutional accountability. The findings reveal the profoundly dangerous environments many secondary students face and provide critical evidence to drive system-level change and strengthen prevention efforts.

### Peer Educator Training Data

As troubling as our Climate Survey findings are, the results from our **[Certified Peer Educator Training](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/become-a-certified-peer-educator/)** offer hope and clear evidence of impact. More than 2,000 students across 45 states have completed the training, demonstrating measurable growth in knowledge, attitudes, and confidence around consent and prevention.

Grounded in youth experiences and aligned with the National Health Education Standards (NHES), the curriculum reflects best practices for school-based prevention while remaining student-driven and survivor-centered. Developed over eight years, the program has become one of the most comprehensive and authentic prevention resources available, endorsed by both students and educators.

# Our Team

SafeBAE is led by a committed team of youth leaders, staff, and board members who bring together lived experience, professional expertise, and a shared dedication to ending sexual violence. As a survivor-founded, youth-led organization, we center the leadership of young people while fostering cross-generational collaboration and advancing cultural change. Our team includes students, educators, advocates, and professionals with backgrounds in public health, education, policy, research, media, and communications. Together, we work to create communities where safety and consent come first — before anything else.

## Leadership Team

[## Shael Norris](https://www.linkedin.com/in/drewthomasdavis/)

Co-Founder & Executive Director

Shael Norris is the Founding Executive Director of SafeBAE, the only national, survivor-founded and youth-led organization in the U.S. dedicated to preventing sexual violence among teens. A lifelong advocate, she began her career as a founding staffer at V-Day, where she oversaw global productions of *The Vagina Monologues* from 1999 to 2016. In 2007, she launched the Campus Accountability Project to push for stronger prevention and response efforts on college campuses. Recognizing the need for early, youth-led intervention, Shael founded SafeBAE in 2015 in partnership with Daisy and Charlie Coleman, Ella Fairon, and Jada Smith. She continues to lead the organization’s national efforts in youth-leadership, consent education, and mental health advocacy.

[## Drew Davis](https://www.linkedin.com/in/drewthomasdavis/)

Director of Strategic Initiatives

Drew Davis is an applied researcher and development strategist dedicated to advancing survivor justice and dismantling systems of harm through youth-led, community-driven approaches. As Director of Strategic Initiatives at SafeBAE, Drew leads development and organizational strategy — building the infrastructure that sustains youth-led programs and expands the organization’s national impact. He oversees major initiatives in prevention education and youth development, with a focus on rigorous data collection, program evaluation, and long-term sustainability, ensuring all initiatives are research-informed and responsive to young people’s needs.

Drew holds a Master of Public Health and a Master of Public Affairs from Brown University, where he concentrated in Black Feminist Health Science Studies, and a B.A. in Individualized Studies and Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, along with a Graduate Certificate in WGS, from Miami University of Ohio.

He is a fellow of the Vermont Network’s Amplify Leadership Lab and serves as an advisor to The Every Voice Coalition, shaping state policy and strengthening support systems for survivors nationwide. Drew has also held roles with Know Your IX, Visible & Resilient, and the National Coalition for Sexual Health. His work on survivor justice and Title IX has been featured in *USA Today*, *YES! Magazine*, *Inside Higher E*d, and *Governing*.

## Aela Mansmann

Director of Programs

Aela Mansmann is the Director of Programs and Outreach at SafeBAE, where she leads national prevention initiatives, strengthens partnerships with schools across the country, and mentors young leaders to create lasting culture change. With nearly a decade of experience in youth advocacy and nonprofit leadership, she brings a track record of building sustainable initiatives that empower and amplify student voices.

At SafeBAE, Aela has expanded digital resources reaching more than 86,000 students, spearheaded peer-led prevention campaigns, and coordinated programming that embeds consent education into school communities nationwide. A two-term Student Body President at Manhattanville University, she revitalized and expanded the Student Government Association, fostering a culture of inclusion, representation, and student-led problem solving on campus.

Her work is grounded in the belief that education, empathy, and grassroots empowerment are the foundation of safer, more equitable communities. She is dedicated to giving young people the tools, platforms, and confidence to lead the change they wish to see.

## Val Odiembo

Youth Engagement Manager

Val Odiembo is a first-year student at Rhode Island College, pursuing a double major in Nursing and Criminal Justice with a passion for public health and violence prevention. A longtime SafeBAE leader, Val is a SafeBAE Youth Board Member and serves as SafeBAE’s Youth Engagement Manager, where she supports the Director of Programs in strengthening youth leadership, expanding student involvement, and supporting SafeBAE club leaders across the country. Val has led SafeBAE clubs at both the Rhode Island Nurses Institute and RIC, presented at statewide health education conferences, and facilitated workshops through the Rhode Island Community Justice Program. Currently, she is organizing a training seminar for Sexual Assault Nurse Examiners (SANEs), deepening her commitment to survivor-centered care and systems change.

## In Memorium

This August marks six years since the passing of Daisy Coleman, SafeBAE’s co-founder. As a teenage survivor, Daisy shared her story in the documentary Audrie & Daisy, speaking openly about what had happened to her and bringing the realities facing young survivors to a national audience. Her vision became the foundation of SafeBAE and helped ignite our youth-led movement.

Daisy was more than her advocacy. She was a tattoo artist whose work people still carry with them, and she was loved deeply by her family and friends. Her example still guides how we show up for students, and her story is carried forward by us and by communities across the country.

### ***[“What Daisy Coleman Changed”](https://www.thecut.com/2020/12/what-daisy-coleman-changed.html#:~:text=All%20the%20organizing%20that%20happened,hashtag%20and%20a%20rallying%20cry.)***

***“All the organizing that happened after Daisy spoke out may not necessarily be a direct result but is certainly a ripple effect:** the new campus anti-rape movement, followed by the backlash over Brock Turner, followed by the sudden ubiquity of MeToo as both a hashtag and a rallying cry.”*

## #ForDaisy Memorial Tribute Wall

Daisy reached people she never met: survivors who saw themselves in her story, students who felt less alone because she spoke first, parents and educators who changed how they show up for young people because of her. When she passed, we collected tribute messages at her memorial service, more than 700 of them, and we have held them close ever since.

Her reach hasn’t stopped. Every year, hundreds of people still find their way to SafeBAE through Daisy’s story and tell us she is the reason they came to this work. Six years later, she is still bringing people in.

This year we built this wall to finally bring those messages together in one place. If Daisy touched your life, whether you knew her personally or only through her work, we invite you to add your own message below.

Send Message

## Remembering Daisy

Below is the statement we shared with our community on the day Daisy passed. With it are photos and recordings from those days, including her virtual memorial service and photos for remembrance. Together they hold both the grief and the celebration of her life, in the words people spoke and the images they gathered in her honor. We’ve kept everything here for anyone who wants to return to it, whether you were there or are only now finding Daisy’s story. You’re welcome to revisit these whenever you’d like.

❮
❯

Read the statement we shared after Daisy's passing

# DAISY COLEMAN

#### MARCH 30TH, 1997 – AUGUST 4TH, 2020

Through our shock and sadness, we are releasing a statement about our loss of Daisy.  As all of our supporters know, Daisy has fought for many years to both heal from her assault and prevent future sexual violence among teens.  She was our sister in this work and much of the driving force behind it.  We were not just a non-profit team, but a family.  We are shattered and shocked by her passing from suicide.  She had been in EMDR therapy for 2 years, working on her triggers and healing from the many traumas in her life.  She had many coping demons and had been facing and overcoming them all, but as many of you know, healing is not a straight path or any easy one.  She fought longer and harder than we will ever know.  But we want to be mindful of all the young survivors who looked up to her.  Please know that above ALL ELSE, she did this work for you.  She loved talking to young people about changing the culture and taking care of one another.  Much of her healing came from each of you.  She was so proud of the work we’ve done and loved seeing so many fierce young activists push for change in their schools and among their friends.  

She would want young survivors to know they are heard, they matter, they are loved, and there are places for them to get the help they need. And she would want everyone else – peer allies, educators, parents, legislators, religious leaders – to come together to help stop sexual violence and help save teen lives. 

As advocates we know survivors of sexual assault are 10 times more likely to attempt suicide than those who haven’t experienced sexual assault, and that is why we will keep dedicating ourselves to this work in her legacy. There’s no question that she would want that.

All of our love,  
SafeBAE

# For Educators

## We know how very much educators are tasked with in any given day, so we have worked to provide tools for all levels of use. Start wherever you can — the most important part is helping your students feel engaged and invited into this work.

### Teaching Guides

Our Teaching Guides are built for short, meaningful discussions and can work well in advisory, health class, homeroom, clubs, or small-group settings. Each guide is paired with a youth-led educational video and includes discussion prompts and classroom activities.

[View Teaching Guides](https://www.safebae.org/resources/teaching-guides/ "Teaching Guides")

### Classroom Posters

Our Posters are easy-to-share educational materials that can help reinforce key messages around consent, healthy relationships, boundaries, and student support. They work well in classrooms, counseling offices, hallways, wellness centers, and student spaces.

[Download Posters](https://www.safebae.org/resources/posters/ "Posters")

### Consent Curriculum

Our Consent Curriculum is designed for deeper, more sustained engagement across multiple class periods. It covers consent, healthy relationships, bystander intervention, and response — with structured lesson plans that can be adapted for different school contexts.

[Learn More](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/consent-curriculum/ "Learn More")

### SafeBAE 360° Schools

Our 360° Schools program is a comprehensive, survivor-centered model that builds lasting prevention infrastructure across your whole school community. It spans education, youth leadership, policy reform, and staff training — flexible enough to start small and grow over time.

[Learn More](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/ "360° Schools")

#### Introducing Vibe Check

## **CheckYourVibe.org**

Vibe Check is a free, anonymous, self-guided tool that helps young people reflect on the health of their relationships. It is designed to be used privately and voluntarily — **it should never be assigned to students.** Making it available as an optional resource allows students who may need it to access it on their own terms, before you know anything specific about their situation.  
Consider sharing the link in your syllabus, on a resource wall, or anywhere students can find it without being asked to engage publicly.

[Explore the Tool](http://checkyourvibe.org "Vibe Check")

[Adult Guide](https://www.safebae.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Check-Their-Vibe-A-Guide-to-Vibe-Check.pdf "Parents")

### For Daisy: Before Anyone Else

## Certified Peer Educator Training

SafeBAE’s Certified Peer Educator Training empowers young people to lead conversations about consent, healthy relationships, and their lived experiences by equipping them with the knowledge, confidence, and leadership skills to drive prevention efforts in their own schools and communities. Whether you’re a student ready to make change or an educator looking to bring youth-led programming into your school, this training is a powerful way to shift school culture from the inside out.

[Register Here](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/become-a-peer-educator/studentregistration/ "Student Registration – Peer Educator Training")

[Ver en Español](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/version-en-espanol/)

[Resume Training](https://learning.www.safebae.org/students)

This training is offered in memory of our co-founder, Daisy Coleman, whose vision and leadership continue to inspire SafeBAE’s mission and youth nationwide. #ForDaisy

## What is the Peer Educator Certification?

SafeBAE’s Certified Peer Educator Training is a free, self-paced training designed for high school students who want to lead sexual violence prevention in their schools and communities. Trauma-informed and accessible from anywhere, the program equips students to educate peers, challenge harmful norms, and build safer school environments.

The certification includes 16 interactive online modules, plus one-on-one support from SafeBAE’s team. Upon completion, students receive an official certification, along with access to ongoing leadership, organizing, and advocacy opportunities.

Peer educators become trusted voices in their schools — facilitating classroom discussions, leading school clubs, organizing events, running social media campaigns, and modeling what consent culture looks like in practice. This training creates a clear pathway for young people to drive cultural change.

## How It Works

**Becoming a Certified Peer Educator is simple, flexible, and fully supported. Students can register and complete the training entirely for free and at their own pace.**

#### 1. Complete the Registration Form

Fill out a short interest form to get started. We’ll send you everything you need to begin the training.

#### 2. Create Your Training Portal Account

Set up your secure account on Podia to unlock all 16 modules and additional resources.

#### 3. Complete 16 Modules

Learn about consent, healthy relationships, digital safety, and more across 16 interactive modules, completed at your own pace.

#### 4. Complete Post-Survey

Share feedback and reflect on what you’ve learned. Your responses help us improve the training and better support future Peer Educators.

#### 5. Earn Your Certificate

After completing all 16 modules and the post-training survey, you’ll receive your official SafeBAE Certified Peer Educator certificate.

#### 6. Start Leading

Put your skills into action by leading presentations, organizing campaigns, or starting a SafeBAE Club. You can also meet with the SafeBAE team to explore next steps.

## Why Peer Education Matters

Prevention only works when it feels real, and for most students, that means hearing it from someone they trust. Peer education brings authenticity, relatability, and lived experience into the conversation.

When youth lead, their peers listen differently. They ask more honest questions. They take ownership. They change behavior not because they were told to, but because they saw someone like them modeling something better.

*Learn more about the impact of youth-led prevention [here](https://www.safebae.org/resources/data-reports/).*

“As I went on in the training, I felt like I could be a more helpful and supportive person and that I would know what to do if something happened to me or anyone I know. I feel confident that I can help people in all sorts of situations and I am more educated on the effects of rape culture.”

— SafeBAE Certified Peer Educator

Rape Culture & Creating a Culture of Respect

Sexual Harassment, Assault, & Rape Defined

Consent is BAE (Before *Anything* Else)

How to Support A Survivor

Reporting Options & Investigation Requirements

Healing After Sexual Assault

## 13

Dating After Experiencing Sexual Violence

## 14

Bystander Intervention (The BAEcode)

## 15

How to Respond If You’ve Been Accused

## 16

Public Speaking & Leading as a Peer Educator

## Start a SafeBAE club at your school

A SafeBAE club is a student-run chapter that brings consent and healthy relationship education to your school. You decide what your chapter does. We provide the training and materials, and our team is a quick email away when you need help. Registration is free.

*Bring SafeBAE to your school for the first time*

# Reform Your School's Sexual Misconduct Policy

Protecting your school community starts with strong, trauma-informed policies. The 2020 Title IX rule issued by the Department of Education was widely recognized as harmful — narrowing protections for survivors, restricting schools’ ability to respond effectively, and putting students at greater risk of further harm. Although new guidelines were introduced in 2024 to restore protections, they were quickly challenged in court and schools nationwide have been forced back under the restrictive 2020 rule.

With the Department of Education weakened and inconsistent in its enforcement, survivors are left vulnerable and districts face heightened legal risks due to vague and harmful federal standards.

That’s why SafeBAE created a **Student Policy Reform Guide** — a step-by-step resource to help you advocate for safer, trauma-informed, and survivor-centered policies in your district. Whether you’re a student, parent, or community stakeholder, you can use this guide to push for clarity, accountability, and real protection in your schools.

We ask only that you register to receive the guide and keep in touch with us about your progress. Together, we can strengthen protections for students and make schools safer across the country — even as federal protections are rolled back.

Schools can engage with one or more core components — Certified Peer Educator Training, a 16-lesson healthy relationship and consent education curriculum, faculty and staff training, and sexual misconduct policy consultation — each contributing to safer, more supportive learning environments.

# Parents & Caregivers

***Support the young people in your life and in your community.***

At SafeBAE, we know that parents, caregivers, and trusted adults play a critical role in shaping how young people understand safety, consent, and relationships. While our work is youth-led, prevention is a whole-community commitment. This page is here to give you tools, resources, and guidance so you can feel prepared to support the teens in your life.

#### SafeBAE’s Executive Director on the award-winning parenting podcast The Longest Shortest Time

#### Introducing Vibe Check

## **CheckYourVibe.org**

As parents and caregivers, we all find ourselves worrying and trying our best to make this world safe for our children. But society, technology, and social media messaging can sometimes make that feel impossible. We all struggled to navigate our childhoods and our kids are no different. Reminding kids that the measure of our character is not that we never make a mistake, but how we respond to learning that we have caused unintended harm. Intimacy is one of the hardest things for anyone to navigate and we need as many tools as possible to help this generation do it better. That’s why we built Vibe Check: to support kids in asking vulnerable questions, navigating relationships, and being the best partners they can be.

[Explore the Tool](http://checkyourvibe.org "Vibe Check")

[Parent Resources](https://www.safebae.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Check-Their-Vibe-A-Guide-to-Vibe-Check.pdf "Parents")

## Support Youth By Getting Them Involved

One of the most powerful things you can do as a parent or caregiver is to connect your student with SafeBAE’s programs. These opportunities allow young people to build leadership skills, learn about consent and healthy relationships, and create change in their schools and communities.

* **Certified Peer Educator Training:** Encourage your student to enroll in our free, virtual, self-paced training that equips them to educate peers on consent, bystander intervention, and digital safety.
* **Bring SafeBAE to Your School:** Ask your school to partner with us through our SafeBAE 360° whole-school model, which includes curriculum, peer educator training, staff development, and policy support.
* **Summer Activist Institute:** Support your student to apply for our annual Summer Activist Institute, an intensive leadership program that prepares youth to lead prevention and advocacy efforts in their own communities.

[Peer Educator Training](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/become-a-peer-educator/ "Become a Peer Educator")

[Start a School Club](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/become-a-chapter-lead/ "Chapter Lead")

[Summer Activist Institute](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/summer-activist-institute/meet-the-fellows/ "Summer Institute")

## Prevention & Early Conversations

Even if it doesn’t always feel like it, young people look to the adults in their lives for cues about healthy relationships, boundaries, and safety. Starting conversations at home, supporting youth leaders in your community, and advocating for safer schools all make a lasting difference.

* Begin practicing lessons of bodily autonomy and respect from the earliest ages.
* Use everyday opportunities (TV shows, news stories, or social media) to spark conversations before harm happens.
* Model open, judgement-free dialogue so your child feels safe confiding in you if something does happen.

* Create a “safe call” policy. Assure your child they can call you anytime they feel unsafe — safety comes before punishment, no matter what.

### Early Ways to Teach Consent

Teaching consent can start at the youngest ages, through simple, everyday choices that reinforce respect and bodily autonomy:

* **Offer alternatives to hugs.** Encourage toddlers to greet adults in ways that feel comfortable to them—waving, blowing a kiss, or saying hello. This builds a lifelong foundation of bodily autonomy.
* **Normalize consent in classrooms.** Teachers can give elementary students options for how they’d like to be greeted, showing that personal boundaries matter everywhere.
* **Use accurate words for anatomy.** Avoid “cute” or made-up words. Using real terms helps children understand there is no shame in their bodies and equips them to clearly communicate if something inappropriate happens.

As children grow, lessons about consent should grow with them. At SafeBAE, we provide age-appropriate tools & resources to help families and educators build on these early conversations year after year.

## Supporting a Survivor

Learning that your child has experienced sexual violence can be overwhelming, frightening, and heartbreaking. You may feel shock, anger, sadness, or even guilt — all of which are normal reactions. In this moment, the most important thing you can do is to center your child’s needs.

It is crucial that you believe your child and reassure them that the assault was not their fault. Help them access the healing services and support they need, and remember that you, too, may need community and resources to process your own feelings.

* Believe first. Validate their disclosure and let them know you are there for them unconditionally.
* Avoid blame. Resist questions that shift responsibility onto your child (“Why were you there?” “What were you wearing?”).
* Seek support. Connect with a rape crisis advocate, counselor, or support group to guide you and your child through options for care, reporting, and healing.
* Care for yourself. Supporting a survivor can be emotionally heavy. Finding your own support system will strengthen your ability to show up for your child.

[Support a Survivor](https://www.safebae.org/resources/support-a-survivor/ "Support A Survivor")

[Healing Resources](https://www.safebae.org/resources/healing/ "Healing")

### Navigating Reporting & Rights

Your instinct may be to report immediately. Instead, listen to your child’s wishes. If they do choose to report, connect first with an advocate. Reporting options may include:

* **Confidential**: Speaking with an advocate or peer educator.
* **Anonymous**: To flag harm without formal investigation.
* **Law Enforcement**: Filing a police report.
* **Title IX**: Filing a school complaint for investigation and safety planning

### Alternative Justice Approaches

Some survivors want to avoid a full Title IX or police investigation but still hope for accountability. They may wish for the person who harmed them to reflect on their actions and understand the impact. This pathway offers an opportunity for individuals who have caused harm to more fully learn about consent, accountability, and the unintended consequences of their behavior — outside of a formal investigation process.

[Accountability Training](https://www.safebae.org/old-360-schools/accountability-training/ "Accountability Training")

# Partners & Press

SafeBAE’s work is made possible by the incredible partnerships we’ve built with schools, researchers, funders, creatives, and youth-serving organizations across the country. We’re proud to collaborate with those who share our commitment to ending sexual violence, amplifying youth leadership, and shifting culture through education, art, media, and policy. Below, you’ll find a selection of our collaborators, recent media features, and opportunities to partner with us.

[Read Our Blog](https://www.safebae.org/blog/ "Blog")

[Request a Program](https://www.safebae.org/request-a-program/ "Request a Program")

### SafeBAE on The Longest Shortest Time

#### **“Preventing Teens from Joining the Manosphere”**

SafeBAE returned to **[The Longest Shortest Time](https://longestshortesttime.com/episode-255-preventing-teens-from-joining-the-manosphere)** for a conversation with Hillary Frank about [**Vibe Check**](https://checkyourvibe.org/), SafeBAE’s free, anonymous reflection tool for young people who are worried they, or a friend, may have crossed a boundary or caused harm. Featuring Drew Davis, SafeBAE’s Director of Strategic Initiatives, the episode explores what happens when teens bring sensitive questions to Reddit, AI tools, or online spaces that can reinforce shame, denial, misogyny, or defensiveness — and how Vibe Check offers a different path toward reflection, accountability, and repair.

#### “Centering Youth Voices: Youth-Led Prevention and Addressing Harm”

SafeBAE Founding Executive Director Shael Norris joined **[The She Matters Podcast](https://www.shematters.ca/podcasts/the-she-matters-podcast/episodes/2149218219)** to discuss youth-led sexual violence prevention, SafeBAE’s founding story, and what it means to meaningfully center young people in this work. The episode also explores SafeBAE’s school-based prevention model, [Certified Peer Educator Training](https://www.safebae.org/resources/peer-educator-training/), and [Vibe Check](https://checkyourvibe.org/), our accountability tool for young people who may have caused harm.

#### Shaping the National Conversation with The Longest Shortest Time

## **“How to Not (Accidentally) Raise a Rapist”**

The first episode of the relaunch of Hilary Frank’s parenting and culture podcast, reframing one of her most downloaded episodes ([*How to Not (Accidentally) Raise a Racist*](https://longestshortesttime.com/episode-116-how-to-not-accidentally-raise-a-racist/)) to spark dialogue about raising young people who respect boundaries and safety. Featuring SafeBAE’s work and Executive Director Shael Norris, the episode explores what actually works when talking to teens about consent and how schools and parents can build a consent-conscious culture.

SafeBAE’s peer-led prevention model was also featured in Hilary Frank’s **New York Times Opinion** piece [*“Our Kids Cannot Learn About Sex Just From Squeamish Gym Teachers”*](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/01/26/opinion/sex-education-consent-middle-school.html) and the accompanying podcast *“[The Most Important Lesson in Sex Ed Isn’t Actually Sex,”](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/27/opinion/sex-education-consent.html)* which highlight why students are the most effective messengers for prevention.

#### “Reducing Tolerance for Sexual Assault”

SafeBAE appeared on *The Measure of Everyday Life* with host Dr. Brian Southwell, discussing the findings of our [published research paper](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10538712.2024.2385468) — and announcing the launch of SafeBAE’s newest resource, [*CheckYourVibe.org*](http://checkyourvibe.org) — a free, anonymous reflection tool designed for young people who are questioning whether they may have caused harm.

### The Totally Preventable Podcast

SafeBAE was featured on [*The Totally Preventable Podcast*](https://strategicprevention.org/totally-preventable/) in the two-part episode *“Blurred Lines,”* a conversation exploring the intersection of alcohol, drugs, and sexual assault alongside experts from RAINN, DanceSafe, Day One, and more. The podcast highlights local voices and prevention leaders working to address behavioral health and social issues across Newport County, offering insight, resources, and practical ways to support safer, healthier communities. Listen to the podcast episode today!

#### “Sexual Violence Prevention in Schools with SafeBAE”

Hosted by Freya Graf, this candid conversation explores building authentic, youth-driven prevention and meeting young people where they are. Featuring SafeBAE, the episode highlights how partnering with students creates systemic change in school environments and fosters cultures of consent.

#### Streaming Now

## Torrey DeVitto on *Celebrity Name That Tune*

Longtime SafeBAE partner and Board Member Torrey DeVitto recently competed on [*Celebrity Name That Tune*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XFQeOEDbN4M) (Season 5, Episode 12) on FOX — and chose SafeBAE as the beneficiary of her winnings. Torrey donated $29,000 to support youth-led sexual violence prevention, bringing SafeBAE’s mission to a national television audience. Her win reflects an ongoing commitment to our work and demonstrates the power of trusted advocates using their platforms to invest directly in prevention, care, and youth leadership. We’re deeply grateful to Torrey for continuing to show up for SafeBAE — both publicly and behind the scenes.

## Media Collaborations & Partner Films

SafeBAE believes in the power of media and storytelling to advance prevention and end sexual assault and dating violence. We’re proud to collaborate on films and creative projects that center survivors and shift culture.

#### Share

#### Raising Voices (Ni una más)

#### Miller's Girl

#### Feature Film Partner

## Disfluency

Disfluency is an award-winning feature film written and directed by [**Anna Baumgarten**](https://www.annabaumgarten.com/) that offers a survivor-centered portrayal of the aftermath of sexual assault, focusing on trauma, memory, and recovery without depicting the assault itself. SafeBAE partnered with the filmmakers to support the film’s educational impact, collaborating on school-based screenings and accompanying prevention and discussion resources for secondary and higher-education settings.

## Training & Education for Professionals

SafeBAE’s commitment to prevention extends beyond students. We regularly work with educators, legal advocates, service providers, parents, caregivers, and community leaders to share our youth-led model and equip adults with the tools to support survivors and embed prevention into everyday practice. Through keynote presentations, workshops, and national webinars, we provide concrete strategies for engaging youth as leaders, building consent-conscious environments, and sustaining systemic change.

# Request a Program

#### Bring SafeBAE to your school, campus or community.

#### Assemblies & One-Time Events

We know many school partners seek one-time assemblies or awareness events as an accessible first step — and we’re happy to offer them. While assemblies alone cannot replace sustained prevention work, they can spark critical conversations and open the door to deeper engagement.

Our assemblies and school events are always co-presented with youth leaders and tailored to be age-appropriate, relevant, and impactful. They are a powerful entry point for schools beginning their partnership with us, and often serve as the starting place for longer-term collaboration.

#### 360° Schools: A Comprehensive Prevention Model

For schools seeking more than one-time events, SafeBAE’s comprehensive 360° Schools program offers a flexible, youth-led approach to building safer school communities. The model includes five core components: peer educator training, a trauma-informed consent curriculum, faculty and staff professional development, policy support, and educational tools to reduce recidivism.

Each component can be delivered individually or be integrated as part of our whole-school approach, tailored to your school’s needs, goals, and capacity.

[Learn More](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/ "SafeBAE 360")

## What School Leaders Say About SafeBAE

Hear from SafeBAE school partner Araceli Martinez, Community Schools Coordinator at Alliance Ted K. Tajima High School, as she reflects on why she brings SafeBAE to her campus and what she’s seen students gain from it.

## Flexible Pricing for School Partners

We believe cost should never be a barrier to prevention. That’s why we offer a flexible, sliding scale pricing model tailored to each school’s needs and capacity. We consider factors like program scope, number of speakers, and travel requirements — always striving to meet partners where they are.

Book a meeting with us to learn more and get started.

# MYTHS, FACTS & STATISTICS

# Let’s debunk the myths about sexual assault.

We want to debunk the myths surrounding sexual assault. Below, we break down the most common myths about sexual violence, look at what the research actually says, and dig into who is most affected — and why so much of this goes unreported.

#### [What causes sexual violence?](#causes)

#### [Why don’t survivors report?](#survivors-report)

#### [Understanding myths vs. facts](#myths-vs-facts)

#### [Who is most at risk?](#who-is-most-at-risk)

## What causes sexual violence?

People blame a lot of things — being under the influence, the clothes someone is wearing, walking alone, flirty behavior, or hooking up with a lot of people. None of these cause sexual violence. It happens when someone chooses to ignore or violate another person’s boundaries and consent.

That choice is often reinforced by rape culture — victim-blaming, harmful stereotypes, peer pressure, media, algorithms, and beliefs about gender, sexuality, power, and entitlement. Prevention means holding people accountable and challenging the culture that excuses harm.

## Why don't survivors report?

If a survivor doesn’t report to the police, it does NOT mean the violence didn’t happen. There are many reasons someone might not come forward:

* It’s emotionally painful, and trauma can make details hard to remember.
* Shame and stigma — fear of being judged, blamed, or “slut-shamed.”
* Fear of not being believed, or that people will defend the perpetrator.
* Fear that nothing will be done — fewer than 2% of reports lead to a conviction.
* Fear of punishment or retaliation, especially for teens.
* Not realizing what happened was abuse in the first place.

## Real Example: Megan Thee Stallion

In 2020, Megan Thee Stallion was harmed by someone she knew. When police arrived, she said she had stepped on glass because she feared the situation could escalate into police violence. After she later spoke out, she was mocked, doubted, and blamed publicly.

Her story shows why reporting is never simple — and why we should never assume silence means nothing happened. Survivors deserve to be believed, supported, and given choices.

# **Myths vs. Facts**

Myths vs. Facts: Sexual Violence

### Masculinity & Male Survivors

Myth

Men are too strong to be assaulted.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Strength does not prevent sexual violence. At least **1 in 6 men** will experience sexual abuse or assault in their lifetime.

Myth

Men always want sex and welcome all sexual advances.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Sexual assault is never wanted. It is a traumatic experience for any survivor, regardless of gender.

Myth

Only gay men commit sexual violence against other men.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Sexual violence is about **power and control**, not sexual orientation. Survivors and perpetrators can be of any gender or identity.

Myth

Men abused by women “got lucky.”

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Sexual violence is never a privilege. Women can—and do—sexually abuse or assault boys and men. Survivors are not “lucky”; they are harmed and exploited.

### Who It Affects & Who Commits It

Myth

“Real rape” is committed by strangers.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Anyone can be a perpetrator—date rape and stranger rape are both rape. Most rapes are committed by someone the victim knows: **92% of female victims** and **74% of male victims** report perpetrators who were acquaintances or intimate partners, and as many as **93% of child sexual abuse survivors** knew their abuser.

Myth

Only women can be raped.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Sexual assault is experienced by people of all genders. **1 out of 10** rape victims is male, and **1 in 2** transgender people are sexually assaulted in their lifetime.

Myth

Sexual assault can’t happen within a marriage or relationship.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Consent is required every time, in every relationship. A relationship—or a past “yes”—is never standing consent. Intimate partner sexual violence is real, harmful, and a crime in all 50 states.

Myth

Sexual violence doesn’t happen to people with disabilities.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

People with disabilities experience sexual violence at far higher rates. People with intellectual disabilities are sexually assaulted at **7 times the rate** of people without disabilities—and their abusers are often people they know and rely on.

### Blame & Believing Survivors

Myth

False claims of rape are common—most are made for revenge, regret, or attention.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

False reporting rates for sexual assault are in the **2–10% range**—the same as other crimes. The far bigger problem is under-reporting: the majority of sexual assaults are never reported to authorities at all.

Myth

Clothing choices, location, and drinking can prevent rape and harassment.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Sexual assault is about **power, not clothing**. This logic holds survivors responsible for their own assaults instead of placing responsibility where it belongs: on perpetrators.

Myth

If they didn’t fight back, it wasn’t really assault.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Freezing is one of the most common trauma responses. Many survivors experience **tonic immobility**—an involuntary reaction that makes it impossible to move or speak. Not fighting back is never consent.

Myth

If it really happened, they would have reported it right away.

Reveal the fact →

Fact

Delayed reporting is the norm, not the exception. Fear, shame, self-blame, and trauma keep many survivors silent for months, years, or forever. A delay says nothing about the truth of what happened.

## Who is most at risk?

Different identities — and the intersections between them — play a big role in the risk of experiencing violence and in access to reporting and healing resources. As you read these statistics, remember that there’s a lack of research on many marginalized groups, so these numbers are subject to change, and this is in no way a comprehensive list.

# Certified Peer Educator Training

## For Daisy: Before Anyone Else

SafeBAE’s Certified Peer Educator Training empowers young people to lead conversations about consent, healthy relationships, and their lived experiences by equipping them with the knowledge, confidence, and leadership skills to drive prevention efforts in their own schools and communities. Whether you’re a student ready to make change or an educator looking to bring youth-led programming into your school, this training is a powerful way to shift school culture from the inside out.

[Register Here](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/become-a-peer-educator/studentregistration/ "Student Registration – Peer Educator Training")

[Ver en Español](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/version-en-espanol/)

[Resume Training](https://learning.safebae.org/students)

This training is offered in memory of our co-founder, Daisy Coleman, whose vision and leadership continue to inspire SafeBAE’s mission and youth nationwide. #ForDaisy

## What is the Peer Educator Certification?

SafeBAE’s Certified Peer Educator Training is a free, self-paced training designed for high school students who want to lead sexual violence prevention in their schools and communities. Trauma-informed and accessible from anywhere, the program equips students to educate peers, challenge harmful norms, and build safer school environments.

The certification includes 16 interactive online modules, plus one-on-one support from SafeBAE’s team. Upon completion, students receive an official certification, along with access to ongoing leadership, organizing, and advocacy opportunities.

Peer educators become trusted voices in their schools — facilitating classroom discussions, leading school clubs, organizing events, running social media campaigns, and modeling what consent culture looks like in practice. This training creates a clear pathway for young people to drive cultural change.

### **Preview the Training**

❮
❯

## How It Works

**Becoming a Certified Peer Educator is simple, flexible, and fully supported. Students can register and complete the training entirely for free and at their own pace.**

#### 1. Complete the Registration Form

Fill out a short interest form to get started. We’ll send you everything you need to begin the training.

#### 2. Create Your Training Portal Account

Set up your secure account on Podia to unlock all 16 modules and additional resources.

#### 3. Complete 16 Modules

Learn about consent, healthy relationships, digital safety, and more across 16 interactive modules, completed at your own pace.

#### 4. Complete Post-Survey

Share feedback and reflect on what you’ve learned. Your responses help us improve the training and better support future Peer Educators.

#### 5. Earn Your Certificate

After completing all 16 modules and the post-training survey, you’ll receive your official SafeBAE Certified Peer Educator certificate.

#### 6. Start Leading

Put your skills into action by leading presentations, organizing campaigns, or starting a SafeBAE Club. You can also meet with the SafeBAE team to explore next steps.

## Why Peer Education Matters

Prevention only works when it feels real, and for most students, that means hearing it from someone they trust. Peer education brings authenticity, relatability, and lived experience into the conversation.

When youth lead, their peers listen differently. They ask more honest questions. They take ownership. They change behavior not because they were told to, but because they saw someone like them modeling something better.

*Learn more about the impact of youth-led prevention [here](https://www.safebae.org/resources/data-reports/).*

“As I went on in the training, I felt like I could be a more helpful and supportive person and that I would know what to do if something happened to me or anyone I know. I feel confident that I can help people in all sorts of situations and I am more educated on the effects of rape culture.”

— SafeBAE Certified Peer Educator

# Race, Rape Culture, and Resistance

SafeBAE was founded by young survivors who understood early on that sexual violence cannot be separated from race, power, and visibility — especially for Black survivors. From the beginning, SafeBAE has challenged the normalization of harm and the silencing of survivors, naming how racism shapes whose experiences are believed, protected, and taken seriously. Our educational resources reflect this long-standing commitment to survivor-led work, racial justice, and education that tells the full story.

As part of this commitment, SafeBAE has expanded our ***[Certified Peer Educator Training](https://www.safebae.org/get-involved/students/become-a-peer-educator/)*** and developed [***Race, Rape Culture, and Resistance***](#learning-series), a learning series centered on Black youth. Together, these resources offer historical context, present-day analysis, and pathways toward healing — grounded in the lived experiences that shaped SafeBAE from the very beginning.

#### Founder Spotlight

## Jada Smith | Co-Founder of SafeBAE

Jada Smith co-founded SafeBAE with a simple but powerful goal: to make sure that what happened to her would never happen to anyone else.

As a Black teenage survivor of sexual violence, Jada’s life was shaped not only by the harm she experienced, but by the way that harm was exploited and circulated online. Images of her unconscious body were shared without consent, sparking the viral hashtag #JadaPose, which turned her assault into a public spectacle and exposed her to widespread cruelty at a moment of profound vulnerability.

Rather than disappearing, Jada made a deliberate and powerful choice: she spoke out. By reclaiming her name, face, and voice, Jada challenged a culture that too often dehumanizes Black girls — treating their pain as entertainment and their bodies as disposable. Her decision helped catalyze a broader movement of survivor-led resistance, as people across the country mobilized in support of Jada through hashtags like #JusticeForJada, #IAmJada, #StandWithJada, and #JadaCounterPose.

**“There’s no point in hiding… Everybody has already seen my face and my body, but that’s not what I am and who I am.” — Jada Smith**

## What to Expect

This learning series includes four lessons. Each lesson builds understanding across history, present-day realities, media, identity, and healing — with a focus on how sexual violence operates in Black communities and what resistance looks like across generations. These resources are intended for youth, educators, and communities seeking culturally grounded tools to understand sexual violence, challenge harmful narratives, and support healing.

[Start the Training](https://learning.www.safebae.org/race-rape-culture-and-resistance "Race, Rape Culture, & Resistance")

Lesson 1 - The History of Racism & Rape Culture

**Topics include:**

* + Sexual violence under U.S. slavery and the denial of consent
  + Post-emancipation racial terror and survivor testimony
  + Racist sexual stereotypes targeting Black women and men
  + Lynching, Jim Crow violence, and legal exclusion
  + Resistance from the Civil Rights era through the modern #MeToo movement

This module traces how racism and rape culture developed together in U.S. history. Learners examine cases such as Celia, the 1866 Memphis Riot testimony of Frances Thompson, the exploitation of Sarah Baartman, and the dismantling of the “Black rapist” myth by Ida B. Wells. It also highlights resistance led by Recy Taylor, Betty Jean Owens, and Tarana Burke, situating #MeToo within a much longer Black feminist lineage.

Lesson 2 - Sexual Violence in the Black Community Today

**Topics include:**

* + Disproportionate rates of sexual violence affecting Black youth
  + Barriers to reporting and mistrust of systems
  + Bias in policing, courts, and schools
  + Hypersexualization and adultification of Black girls
  + Media stereotypes and school discipline disparities

This module focuses on how historical racism shows up in Black survivors’ lives today. Using current data and lived examples, learners explore why reporting can feel unsafe or harmful, and how stereotypes continue to shape responses to Black pain. The module includes a contemporary case study of Megan Thee Stallion, alongside discussions of dress codes, adultification bias, and the erasure of Black childhood — especially for Black girls and LGBTQ+ youth.

Lesson 3 - Black Boys & Men: Supporting Male Survivors

**Topics include:**

* + Historical myths portraying Black men as sexual threats
  + Lynching, false accusations, and racial terror
  + Consent, boundaries, and the silencing of Black boys
  + Toxic masculinity, stigma, and mental health impacts
  + Public survivor disclosures and pathways to support

This module centers Black boys and men as survivors, challenging the myth that they are only perpetrators or “always want sex.” Learners examine the deadly consequences of racist stereotypes through the murder of Emmett Till, and explore how stigma prevents many boys from being believed or supported. The module also highlights survivor voices from Reggie Walker, Terry Crews, and Lil Wayne, showing how speaking out can help dismantle shame and open doors to healing.

Lesson 4 - Relationships & Sexual Violence in Black Media

**Topics include:**

* + Media representation and its impact on beliefs about relationships
  + Victim-blaming and the “fast” stereotype
  + Abuse portrayed as comedy or normalized behavior
  + Generational trauma and silence
  + Survivor storytelling through music and film

This module analyzes how Black relationships and sexual violence are portrayed in popular media — and how those portrayals shape real-world attitudes. Learners engage with examples from film and music, including *Divorce in the Black*, *Woman Thou Art Loosed*, and *Don’t Be a Menace*, as well as lyrical storytelling from Kendrick Lamar, Jay-Z and Beyonce, and Raye. The module encourages critical reflection on what media teaches about consent, credibility, and whose pain is taken seriously.

# Supporting a Survivor

Healing after sexual violence is deeply personal, with no single path forward. Many survivors find strength in connection — whether with peers, supportive communities, or professionals. These relationships can ease feelings of isolation, reduce guilt or shame, and provide tools for coping. Even when survivors understand they are not to blame, it often takes time and support to fully believe it.

For some, reconnecting with their body and emotions may feel overwhelming. Some survivors experience disconnection or turn to risky behaviors to manage pain. While facing these feelings can be difficult, avoiding them can cause further harm. With compassionate support and mental health resources, survivors can begin to process trauma, reclaim safety, and move toward healing.

Relationships and intimacy after assault can bring new challenges. Survivors may face triggers that complicate dating, while partners may feel uncertain about how to provide support. To open space for these conversations, SafeBAE partnered with *Teen Vogue* to produce [***Dating After Sexual Assault*.**](https://www.safebae.org/resources/videos/dating-a-survivor/) The short video and teaching guide affirm that healing looks different for everyone and offer practical tools for navigating trust, communication, and boundaries, creating space for survivors and partners to explore healthy intimacy after trauma.

### If you’d like immediate support from a trained professional, you can text **‘loveis’ to 22522**

## When Someone Tells You They’ve Been Assaulted

**Opening up about sexual violence takes tremendous courage. If someone chooses to share their experience with you, here’s how to show up for them:**

* **Start by believing.** The single best way to support a survivor is to believe them. Questioning their account — even out of shock — can be devastating and may keep them from ever opening up again.
* **Listen more than you speak.** Show you’re engaged: make eye contact, don’t interrupt, and let them share as much or as little as they want. You don’t need details to be helpful — never press for them.
* **Validate their feelings.** If they minimize what happened (“other people have it worse”), gently remind them they’re allowed to be as upset as they need to be. No assault is “not bad enough” to matter.
* **Meet immediate needs first.** Before processing emotions, make sure they feel physically safe and cared for. Something as simple as a glass of water, a snack, a cozy blanket, or asking if they want a hug can signal to their brain that they’re safe now.
* **Let them lead.** Follow their choices about whether to report, who to tell, and how to cope. Reporting can be re-traumatizing, so never pressure them to. You can help them understand their options while respecting whatever they decide.

Try Saying:
“I’m so sorry this happened to you.”
“You are not alone. I know there are people that can help.”
“How can I support you?”
“It’s not your fault.”
“I’m glad you felt safe to tell me so I can be here for you.”
“You didn’t deserve that to happen to you.”

Don’t Say:
“Why didn’t you just leave?”
“Why were you there?”
“If you kissed, you should have known something was going to happen.”
“Were you drinking?”  “What were you wearing?”
“It’s going to be fine; just move on.”
“If it was really a big deal, why didn’t you tell me sooner?”

# What is Title IX?

Title IX is a federal civil rights law that protects students from sex discrimination in schools and guarantees the right to an education free from harassment, assault, and inequity. Every student deserves to know these protections exist.

**So, what does it do?**

* **Prohibits Discrimination:** Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination in any school or educational program that receives federal funding.
* **Protects All Students:** Title IX protections apply to all students, regardless of gender identity or expression.
* **Covers Various Issues:** Title IX covers a wide range of issues, including sexual harassment, assault, and other forms of gender-based violence.

# Timeline of Title IX

1972

## Title IX Enacted

Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 is signed into law, prohibiting sex-based discrimination in any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.

1977

## Alexander v. Yale

A group of students filed a lawsuit against Yale University, arguing that the university’s failure to address sexual harassment constituted a violation of Title IX. This was the first case to use Title IX to argue that sexual harassment is a form of sex discrimination.

1992

## Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools

This landmark decision marked the first successful interpretation of Title IX to cover sexual harassment, significantly strengthening the law’s enforcement and protections against gender-based discrimination in educational settings.

2011

## The “Dear Colleague” Letter

The Obama administration’s Office for Civil Rights issues the “Dear Colleague” Letter, clarifying that sexual violence is a form of sexual harassment prohibited by Title IX and outlining schools’ responsibility to respond promptly and equitably to reports of sexual violence.

2017

## Rescission of 2011 Guidance

The 2011 guidance is rescinded by the Trump/DeVos administration, and interim guidance is provided, allowing schools more flexibility in handling sexual violence cases and decreasing protections for survivors.

2020

## The Trump/DeVos Title IX Rules

In May 2020, new Title IX regulations are published. These regulations require schools to follow specific procedures for investigating and adjudicating sexual harassment and assault cases, including live hearings and cross-examinations. These rules make it harder for survivors to get the support they need.

2022

## Proposed Title IX Rule

After over a year of pressure from organizers, the Biden administration proposes new changes to the Title IX regulations on June 23, 2022 (the 50th anniversary of Title IX) to better protect students and ensure fair processes. These changes aimed to address some of the criticisms of the 2020 rules.

2024

## Final Rule Update

New Title IX rules are finalized and released on April 19, 2024, and take effect August 1, 2024. These rules provided enhanced protections for students and survivors, including LGBTQ+ students and pregnant and postpartum students.

January 9, 2025

## Vacatur and Post-Decision Status

A federal district court issues a decisive ruling that vacates the 2024 Final Rule in its entirety. The Department of Education has confirmed that the 2024 Title IX regulations and related resources are not effective in any jurisdiction — meaning the 2020 regulations are the rules schools must follow today.

June 16, 2026

## Civil Rights Enforcement Moves to the DOJ

The U.S. Department of Education moves civil rights enforcement from OCR to the Department of Justice, shifting how harassment and discrimination complaints in K-12 schools and colleges are investigated and resolved — and making it even more confusing for students and families to understand where and how to seek justice.

Today

## What Comes Next?

The future of Title IX and its enforcement at the federal level remains uncertain — and yet students still have the legal right to be protected in their schools!

‹
›

### Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972

##### ***“No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.”***

## Title IX Explained

# Is my school covered by Title IX?

Take the 2-question quiz

Do you attend a public or private school?

Public
Private

Unsure

**Here’s how to find out:**
Your school’s website likely lists this information under its “About Us” page or pages discussing its history, mission, or governance. You can also check your student handbook, enrollment forms, or ask a teacher or administrator.

Does your school receive *any* federal funding?

Yes
No

**Here’s how to find out:**
Information about your school’s funding sources can likely be found in its annual reports, budgets, or financial statements. You can also check usaspending.gov or see if your school’s tax statements are available online. If you’re not able to find this information online, you can ask a school administrator, guidance counselor, or teacher.

Your school IS covered by Title IX

That means your school is legally required to prevent and respond to sex-based discrimination — including sexual harassment and assault — so every student has equal access to education.

Your school is NOT covered by Title IX

Private schools that receive no federal funding aren’t bound by Title IX. But your school may still have its own anti-discrimination and safety policies — check your student handbook or ask an administrator about your rights and protections.

Start over

## Supportive Measures

Schools are required to offer supportive measures to students impacted by any form of sex discrimination, including sexual harassment and sexual assault. Students and families can request supportive measures even if they choose to not have an investigation.

### FAQs Brought to You by Our Friends

[Supportive Measures FAQ - K-12](https://nwlc.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/Supportive-Measures-FAQ-K12-vF.pdf)

**Explore SafeBAE’s latest blog posts and social media explainers on Title IX, school accountability, and student rights.**

## Schools Can Do More!

Since 2020, schools have been pulled back and forth between restrictive rules, attempts at expanded protections, and ongoing court challenges. This leaves survivors with fewer options, and schools without clear or consistent guidance. That’s why knowing about Title IX is important, but not enough on its own. **Your school has the power to do better.**

We created the **[School Policy Reform Guide](https://www.safebae.org/360-schools/school-policy-reform-guide/)** to help students, educators, and administrators strengthen policies beyond the bare federal minimum. By adopting trauma-informed, survivor-centered practices, schools can ensure real safety, transparency, and accountability.
