# BAEcode: A Teaching Guide for GAME ON!

# Teaching Bystander Intervention

BAEcode was created to disrupt the familiar “Bro Code” — the idea that we only look out for our own friends or social group. Instead, BAEcode envisions a culture where we all hold each other accountable for kindness, step up when we see harm, and intervene to keep one another safe.

We launched this campaign during Sexual Assault Awareness Month in 2018 to give teens the tools and confidence to practice bystander intervention. By teaching and empowering young people to step in, we aim to prevent sexual harassment and assault within their own peer groups — and shift the culture toward care and accountability.

## What is BAEcode?

Watch out for everyone’s safety — not just your close friends.

Never pressure someone into sexual activity of any kind.

Don’t ever send unrequested nude photos.

Always get enthusiastic consent before & during any sexual activity.

### GAME ON! is the centerpiece of BAEcode, our bystander intervention campaign.

Created *with teens, for teens* by SafeBAE co-founder Ella Fairon, the short film portrays everyday situations and gives young people simple, practical strategies to step in — whether in-person or online. The entire production team — writing, producing, directing, and casting — was made up of high school and college students.

We know that middle and high schoolers have the power and responsibility to change the conversation, shift culture, and build communities that are safe and free from sexual violence.

[Watch GAME ON!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BCqkJSXCu-E "Teaching Guide")

“The idea is simple: many cases of sexual violence can be prevented or stopped if an alert bystander intervenes in time.” – Ella Fairon | Director

## Why Teach Bystander Intervention?

Bystander (or **BAE\*stander**) intervention is one of the most effective tools we have to engage *everyone* in the prevention of sexual harassment and assault. The idea is simple: many cases of sexual and dating violence can be stopped if an alert bystander steps in.

If someone at a party notices another person being pressured, isolated, or taken advantage of, they can interrupt the situation and potentially prevent a sexual assault from happening. But without talking openly about it and giving people practical ways to act, most will do nothing. Intervening can feel intimidating even for adults — and for young people, the social pressure and uncertainty of “what to do” can make it even harder.

That’s why teaching bystander skills is so important. Research shows that when teens learn concrete strategies to step in, rates of harassment and assault go down. The **BAEcode Facilitator Guide** uses the *GAME ON!* campaign to help identify risky situations and introduce creative strategies for safe intervention. One of BAEcode’s core principles is that *everyone* can learn to de-escalate situations where consent has not, or cannot, be given. While *GAME ON!* highlights distraction and de-escalation tactics on screen, classroom discussions often bring up other useful strategies as well.

### JAMA Pediatrics, March 2018

**15% of teens under 18** years old reporting that they **send nudes**, **27% receive them**, and another **12% forward them**.

An analysis of **500 accounts from 12 to 18-year-old girls** about negative experiences sexting found that **2/3rds of them had been asked to provide explicit images** — and that the requests often **progressed from promises of affection to “anger displays, harassment and threats.”**

# Online Harassment of Survivors

Online harassment and disbelief of survivors is a widespread issue that many survivors describe as being as harmful — or even more harmful — than the assault itself. The inability to escape rumors, victim-blaming, and shaming at school and on social media can cause long-lasting trauma, including suicidal ideation. This teaching guide is designed to help peers understand the impact of online harassment, recognize how harmful language and behaviors contribute to revictimization, and practice supportive responses that affirm and protect survivors.

Our youth leaders created *#QuitThisShit* in 2016 as part of a social media campaign to break the cycle of online revictimization. The script for this video draws from real messages survivors have received and may not be appropriate for all school settings. As part of this campaign, we also offer a non-explicit short film, [*Help Put an End to the Online Harassment of Survivors.*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-I4Jmz7Yxys&list=PLcjnufC_d_R_B8EyxCCIVFhJIbMRI_HQj&index=5)

# Rape Culture & How to Shift to a Culture of Respect

This teaching guide provides educators with discussion prompts, activities, and facilitation tips to help students recognize how rape culture shows up in everyday life and take action to create cultural change. Paired with a short film featuring SafeBAE co-founder Charlie Coleman, the guide gives students concrete steps for challenging harmful norms and building a culture rooted in equity, consent, and accountability.

## What is rape culture?

Rape culture refers to the values, attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors that trivialize or normalize sexual violence. From victim-blaming and harmful media portrayals to peer pressure and gender stereotypes, these norms allow violence to persist. But students can be part of shifting the narrative — from a culture that excuses harm to one built on respect and consent.

## Vibe Check by SafeBAE

#### No Judgement. Just Answers.

SafeBAE has launched [CheckYourVibe.org](http://checkyourvibe.org/), a free, anonymous reflection tool designed for young people who are questioning whether they may have crossed a boundary or caused harm.

Young people are increasingly turning to anonymous forums and AI chatbots to ask difficult questions about relationships and consent. But AI is designed to tell you what you want to hear — not help you reflect or take accountability. Vibe Check guides users through confusing situations and connects them with real, evidence-based resources on consent, communication, and accountability — not AI advice.

[Explore the Tool](http://checkyourvibe.org "Vibe Check")

#### “Preventing Teens from Joining the Manosphere”

Drew Davis joins Hillary Frank on [The Longest Shortest Time](https://longestshortesttime.com/episode-255-preventing-teens-from-joining-the-manosphere) to talk about [Vibe Check](http://checkyourvibe.org), the rise of AI and online forums as relationship advice spaces, and why young people need better pathways to reflect, take accountability, and repair harm.

Where are young people learning how to think about relationships, consent, accountability, and repair?
Increasingly, many are turning to AI tools, Reddit forums, influencers, or online communities that frame these experiences through blame, defensiveness, misogyny, punishment, or emotional isolation. That concerns me deeply, especially for young men who are already struggling with loneliness, confusion, and a lack of healthy relational guidance.
I recently came across Vibe Check, a new project from SafeBAE, and I think it represents something genuinely important.
Vibe Check is a free and fully anonymous reflection tool designed for young people who are questioning whether they or a friend may have crossed a boundary, caused harm, or handled a situation poorly.
Instead of escalating shame or encouraging denial, the tool walks users through reflection, accountability, empathy, communication, and repair. Importantly, it is intentionally not AI-generated. It was built from years of direct work with young people around consent, relationships, and sexual violence prevention.
What I appreciate most is that it recognizes something many conversations miss: Accountability is relational.
People rarely grow through humiliation alone. Growth often happens when individuals are given structured opportunities to reflect honestly, understand impact, reconnect to others, and move toward repair.
That does not minimize harm. It creates conditions where accountability is more likely to happen.
At a time when so many young people are searching online for answers about deeply human situations, I think tools like this matter.
